chunks.content: Introduction The equilibrium and interplay among vaginal microorganisms are of utmost importance for maintaining optimal vaginal health in women. Lactobacillus, which is the predominant microorganism found in the vaginal microbiota of the majority of healthy women, assumes a crucial function in safeguarding the host against infections in the reproductive tract [ ]. Bacterial vaginosis occurs when the presence of polymicrobial flora, such as bacteria from the genera Gardnerella, Atopobium, Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus, Mobiluncus, Sneathia, Leptotrichia, or Mycoplasma, is observed in the absence of vaginal lactobacilli [ ]. The occurrence of hormonal changes during pregnancy is associated with a heightened prevalence of vaginitis. Specifically, oestrogen diminishes the resistance of vaginal epithelial cells towards pathogens [ , ], while progesterone enhances the adhesion of pathogens to the vaginal epithelium [ ]. Moreover, both oestrogen and progesterone may amplify the virulence of pathogenic strains [ ]. The prevalence of bacterial vaginosis (BV) during pregnancy exhibits considerable variation, ranging from 3.54% to 50.0%, and is contingent upon the specific population under investigation [ ]. Research suggests that there is an association between BV and adverse reproductive outcomes in pregnant women, as well as complications in neonates [ – ]. Induction of labour (IOL) is a common obstetric practice that refers to the process of medically and surgically initiating uterine contractions before natural labour begins [ ]. Induced labour is presently regarded as one of the most commonly conducted obstetric interventions, as approximately 25% of pregnancies reaching full term necessitate the need for inductio [ – ]. The indications for inducing labour primarily stem from medical, maternal, or foetal factors but may also encompass social and nonmedical considerations, such as convenience or maternal preference. As the frequency of these indications escalates, it is anticipated that the incidence of induced labour will persistently increase [ , ]. Nevertheless, the failure to induce labour is a prevalent occurrence, with an incidence rate of up to 20% [ ] and can result in diverse complications for both the mother and the infant [ ]. Insufficient research has been conducted regarding bacterial vaginosis (BV) during the third trimester of pregnancy and its association with induced labour, leaving the correlation between BV during this period and caesarean section following induced labour, as well as the potential impact on maternal and foetal outcomes, uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate maternal and infant outcomes following induced labour for bacterial vaginosis (BV) detected prior to induction. The primary objective was to examine the hypothesis that women with BV may encounter more adverse outcomes during induced labour. Methods Participants This retrospective study aimed to gather data on the induction of labour in the obstetrics department at Anhui Maternal and Child Health Hospital, specifically focusing on singleton nulliparous women. The data collection period spanned from January 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023. Additional inclusion criteria for the study included participants who were between the ages of 18 and 45 years, had an intrauterine pregnancy, were at least 37 weeks pregnant, had intact foetal membranes, presented with a cephalic presentation, and exhibited a normal foetal heart rate. The exclusion criteria for this study included individuals with a history of sexually transmitted infections, recent vaginal bleeding or antibiotic usage within the past month, recent sexual intercourse or vaginal medication usage within the past three days, vulvar dermatology conditions, known autoimmune diseases, cephalopelvic disproportion, placenta previa, cervical cerclage, premature rupture of membranes, mental or intellectual abnormalities,, as well as the utilization of double balloons for labour induction. Specimen collection and processing Following admission, the initial step involved the examination of vaginal secretions, followed by a thorough assessment of the birth canal and cervix through vaginal examination. A medical sampling swab (Jiangsu Kangjie Medical Devices Co., Ltd, China) was utilized to collect vaginal secretion samples from the lateral wall of the upper third of the vagina and the posterior fornix. These samples were then subjected to vaginal pH measurement using special test paper (pH 3.8–5.4; Shanghai SSS Reagent Co., Ltd, China) and examined under a microscope (Olympus, Japan) at a magnification of ×400. Following the speculum examination, pertinent observations were made regarding the vaginal discharge (including the quantity, colour, appearance, and smell), the condition of the vaginal mucosa (such as redness, ulceration, and swelling), and the identification of hyperaemic or purulent discharge in the cervix. The sample was applied onto a microscope slide and combined with a small amount of saline solution, after which the slide was promptly subjected to microscopic examination. Diagnostic criteria BV is diagnosed based on the Amsel criteria [ ] which require the presence of at least three out of the following four indicators: ① grey, homogeneous, and thin vaginal secretions; ② vaginal secretions with a pH value greater than 4.5; ③ a positive amine test; and ④ more than 20% of vaginal epithelial cells identified

redness, ulceration, and swelling), and the identification of hyperaemic or purulent discharge in the cervix. The sample was applied onto a microscope slide and combined with a small amount of saline solution, after which the slide was promptly subjected to microscopic examination. Diagnostic criteria BV is diagnosed based on the Amsel criteria [ ] which require the presence of at least three out of the following four indicators: ① grey, homogeneous, and thin vaginal secretions; ② vaginal secretions with a pH value greater than 4.5; ③ a positive amine test; and ④ more than 20% of vaginal epithelial cells identified as clue cells by wet slide microscopy. Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is diagnosed upon the identification of blastospores or pseudohyphae of the fungus through microscopic examination [ ]. Furthermore, as a standard procedure, the evaluation of the presence of Trichomonas vaginalis is conducted [ ]. However, the analysis excluded all patients diagnosed with trichomoniasis due to the limited sample size. Study group assignment The patients were categorized into two groups, namely, the BV group and the nonvaginitis group, based on the outcomes of the vaginal discharge test. The study comprised two groups: the BV group, consisting of individuals with bacterial vaginosis, and the BV + VVC group, consisting of individuals with both bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis. Pregnant women exhibiting normal vaginal secretions were included in the nonvaginitis group. Induction methods In accordance with the established protocol of our academic institution, experienced obstetricians prescribed induction techniques based on Bishop scores, which encompassed the utilization of the insertion of a dinoprostone plug and the combined approach of amniotomy with oxytocin. Dinoprostone (Propess, Switzerland) was administered intravaginally in the posterior fornix while monitoring contractions and the foetal heart rate. The drug was discontinued if contractions became excessive or too frequent or if the Bishop score exceeded 6 points. Oxytocin(H32025280, Nanjing Xinbai Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., China) was employed in cases of ineffective uterine contractions or slow labour progression. Oxytocin was administered to initiate productive uterine contractions, characterized by 3–4 contractions of 200 Montevideo units within a 10-minute interval. When the Bishop score reached 6 points, amniotomy was performed in conjunction with oxytocin administration. The outcome of induced labour The maternal outcome measures encompassed a range of indicators, namely, caesarean section, chorioamnionitis, postpartum haemorrhage, blood transfusion, artificial placenta dissection, postpartum urinary retention, puerperal infection, lateral episiotomy, and severe perineal laceration. The neonatal outcomes examined in this study encompassed meconium-contaminated amniotic fluid (MSAF), neonatal asphyxia, neonatal infection, and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). Chorioamnionitis (CAM) is histologically characterized by the existence of acute inflammatory lesions in either the chorion or amniotic membrane, as per the Blanc criteria [ ]. These criteria consist of stage I (subchorionitis), which involves the presence of numerous dispersed neutrophil infiltrates in the chorionic plate or membranous chorionic connective tissue, and stage III (CAM), which entails neutrophil infiltrates extending to the subamniotic connective tissue and amniotic epithelium. The diagnosis of clinical chorioamnionitis (CAM) can be established when a patient presents with a fever equal to or exceeding 38 °C, does not have any apparent infection, and has at least one of the following signs or symptoms: a maternal pulse rate equal to or exceeding 100 beats per minute, uterine tenderness, foul vaginal discharge, or a maternal white blood cell count equal to or exceeding 15 × 109/L [ ]. Puerperal infection, also known as postpartum infection, pertains to the invasion of the reproductive tract by pathogens during childbirth and the postpartum period, resulting in either localized or systemic infection [ ]. Puerperal infections encompass a combination of two or more clinical manifestations, namely, pelvic pain, fever, atypical vaginal discharge, malodorous discharge, or delayed uterine involution [ ]. Neonatal asphyxia was operationally defined as the confluence of several criteria, including the presence of risk factors for neonatal asphyxia, an Apgar score of 7 or lower at either 1–5 min after birth, an umbilical artery pH below 7.15, and the exclusion of alternative causes for a low Apgar score [ ]. Neonatal infection was characterized by laboratory confirmation of bacterial infection and/or the manifestation of clinical indicators of infection [ ]. The evaluation of early neonatal infection adhered to the criteria established by the World Health Organization (WHO), which encompassed the identification of at least one of the following signs: temperature instability, lethargy, feeding intolerance, respiratory distress, haemodynamic instability, convulsions, hypotonia, irritability, or haemorrhagic diathesis [ ]. The acquisition of pertinent data was carried out by accessing electronic medical records systems and microbiology reports. In adherence to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, the Biomedical Ethics Committee of Anhui Medical University granted approval for the execution of this study (Ethics No.: 83230472). The acquisition of pertinent data was carried out by accessing electronic medical records systems and microbiology reports. In adherence to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, the Biomedical Ethics Committee of Anhui Medical University granted approval for the execution of this study (Ethics No.: 83230472). Statistical analysis The data analysis was conducted using SPSS software (version 23.0) developed by SPSS, Inc. in Chicago, IL, USA. The normality of quantitative data was assessed using the one-sample Shapiro‒Wilk test. Any data that deviated from a normal distribution were represented as the median (25th to 75th percentile) [M(P25 ~ P75)], and a nonparametric test (Mann‒Whitney U test) was employed. The count data are presented as the number of cases and corresponding percentages. The X2 test or Fisher’s exact probability method was employed for statistical analysis. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Logistic regression analysis was employed to evaluate the potential of BV as a risk factor for adverse maternal and infant outcomes. Univariate analysis identified significant associations between BV and various adverse outcomes, such as caesarean delivery, PPH, blood transfusion, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, chorioamnionitis, postpartum urinary retention, puerperal infection, admission to the NICU, and neonatal infection. These outcomes were selected as dependent variables, while BV was considered an independent variable. Additionally, maternal age, BMI, Bishop score, history of vaginitis during pregnancy, mode of induction and birth weight were included as covariates. The unadjusted odds ratio, adjusted odds ratio (OR) and corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI) were computed. Results Sociodemographic description of the study population Figure illustrates the screening process conducted on a total of 474 pregnant women, who were categorized into two groups: the BV group ( n = 166) and the nonvaginitis group ( n = 301). Within the BV group, there were 98 women with BV and 34 women with BV coexisting with vulvovaginal candidiasis (BV + VVC). Basic clinical data Table presents the general clinical data of the 132 pregnant women diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis (BV) and 342 pregnant women without vaginitis. There were significant differences observed between the BV group and the nonvaginitis group in terms of BMI, Bishop score, birth weight, and mode of labour induction ( p = 0.028, p = 0.002, p = 0.000, p = 0.003). However, there were no significant differences found between the two groups in terms of maternal age (years), weight before induction, gestational age at induction (weeks), gravidity, AFI (mm), haemoglobin levels, educational level, smoking status, history of vaginitis during pregnancy, Group B Streptococcus infection, anaemia, or induction of labour (all P > 0.05). In comparison to the BV + VVC group, in the BV group, a statistically significant disparity was observed in the occurrence of vaginitis during pregnancy ( p = 0.000). However, no statistically significant distinctions were found in other general clinical data ( P > 0.05). Induction of labour Table presents the findings indicating that the BV group exhibited a greater prevalence of CS and a lower prevalence of VD in comparison to the nonvaginitis group (24.24% vs. 11.99%; 75.76% vs. 88.01%; P = 0.001, respectively). There were significant differences in CS indications between the two groups. The incidence of chorioamnionitis was found to be significantly greater in the bacterial vaginosis (BV) group than in the nonvaginitis group, with rates of 12.50% and 0.00%, respectively. The BV group exhibited significantly higher rates of PPH, blood transfusion, chorioamnionitis, postpartum urinary retention, puerperal infection, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, neonatal infection, and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit ( p < 0.001 for all variables, except puerperal infection ( p = 0.017)). There were no statistically significant differences observed in the occurrence of artificial separation of the placenta, lateral episiotomy, epidural analgesia, or asphyxia neonatorum between the two groups, as indicated by a p value greater than 0.05. In comparison to the single BV group, the BV + VVC group showed higher rates of postpartum bleeding, postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), blood transfusion, chorioamnionitis, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, neonatal infection ( n ,%) and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit ( n ,%) ( p = 0.002, p = 0.001, p = 0.001, p = 0.000, p = 0.014, p = 0.014, respectively). There was no statistically significant difference observed in the other outcomes of induced labour ( P > 0.05). Multivariate analysis of adverse maternal and child outcomes Table shows a multivariate analysis of adverse maternal and child outcomes. After adjusting for various factors, such as age, BMI, Bishop score, history of vaginitis in pregnancy, mode of induction and birth weight, it was found that both the BV group and nonvaginitis group had

to the neonatal intensive care unit ( n ,%) ( p = 0.002, p = 0.001, p = 0.001, p = 0.000, p = 0.014, p = 0.014, respectively). There was no statistically significant difference observed in the other outcomes of induced labour ( P > 0.05). Multivariate analysis of adverse maternal and child outcomes Table shows a multivariate analysis of adverse maternal and child outcomes. After adjusting for various factors, such as age, BMI, Bishop score, history of vaginitis in pregnancy, mode of induction and birth weight, it was found that both the BV group and nonvaginitis group had a higher risk of adverse maternal and child outcomes, including caesarean delivery, PPH, blood transfusion, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, chorioamnionitis, postpartum urinary retention, puerperal infection, admission to the NICU, and neonatal infection. These differences were statistically significant( P <0.05). Discussion The purpose of this study was to examine maternal and foetal outcomes after induced labour in the third trimester in women with BV. The results of our study indicate that women diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis (BV) face a significantly higher likelihood of experiencing various adverse outcomes during childbirth. Specifically, after accounting for potential confounding variables, it was observed that women with BV had a twofold increased risk of undergoing caesarean section following induction in comparison to those with a healthy vaginal flora (odds ratio [OR] 2.319, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.508–3.566). Additionally, these individuals exhibited a greater incidence of postpartum haemorrhage, blood transfusion, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, chorioamnionitis, postpartum urinary retention, puerperal infection, admission to the NICU, and neonatal infection. Furthermore, when comparing BV alone to BV with VVC, no significant disparity was observed in the caesarean section rate following induction. However, women with both BV and VVC exhibited a higher prevalence of postpartum haemorrhage, transfusion, chorioamnionitis, meconium contamination of amniotic fluid, neonatal infection, and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit. In recent years, a multitude of scholarly investigations have been conducted concerning BV and its potential correlation with unfavourable reproductive outcomes. These studies have indicated that the presence of BV during pregnancy is linked to a heightened occurrence of premature rupture of membranes (PROM), premature delivery, perinatal infections, and neonatal infections [ – , ]. In a comprehensive meta-analysis involving a sample size of 30,518 women from 32 distinct studies, a statistically significant correlation was observed between bacterial vaginosis (BV) and adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth (odds ratio [OR] 2.16, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.56 to 3.00), late abortion (OR: 6.32, 95% CI: 3.65 to 10.94), and maternal infection (OR 2.53, 95% CI; 1.26 to 5.08) [ ]. In a more recent study, Haahr et al. found that the presence of bacterial vaginosis (BV) at 24 weeks gestation was linked to a notably higher likelihood of emergency caesarean delivery (odds ratio [OR] 1.37, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15–1.64, p < 0.001) [ ]. While numerous studies have established a robust correlation between bacterial vaginosis (BV) and unfavourable reproductive outcomes, limited research has been conducted to examine the impact of BV during pregnancy on induced labour outcomes. We exclusively surveyed primiparas due to the potential inadequacy of studying both induced multiparas and primiparas as a research strategy. Previous research has brought attention to the limited predictive value of the Bishop score in determining the success of induction and the potential for adverse outcomes in multiparous women. Additionally, these studies have suggested that regardless of their initial Bishop scores, multiparous women can undergo induction safely and have successful outcomes [ ]. Our research successfully gathered comprehensive data on bacterial vaginosis (BV) in women who underwent induced labour during the third trimester of pregnancy. Current pregnancy care guidelines suggest routine screening for bacterial vaginosis (BV), vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC), trichomoniasis, and aerobic vaginitis (AV) in pregnant women exhibiting symptoms in the lower genital tract. However, there remains a contentious debate regarding the necessity of routine screening for these infections in asymptomatic women [ ]. Although women with BV can present with symptoms, BV is predominantly characterized as a subclinical condition, frequently manifesting as an asymptomatic disease [ ]. Hence, acquiring comprehensive data on bacterial vaginosis (BV) during pregnancy poses a challenge. Nevertheless, the customary practice of conducting screenings for vaginal infections in pregnant women prior to induction during the third trimester ensures that we possess a relatively comprehensive dataset. The findings of our study indicate that women diagnosed with BV exhibited a roughly twofold increased risk of undergoing caesarean section after induced labour. Additionally, these women experienced a greater occurrence of unfavourable maternal and foetal outcomes when compared to those with a normal vaginal flora. women prior to induction during the third trimester ensures that we possess a relatively comprehensive dataset. The findings of our study indicate that women diagnosed with BV exhibited a roughly twofold increased risk of undergoing caesarean section after induced labour. Additionally, these women experienced a greater occurrence of unfavourable maternal and foetal outcomes when compared to those with a normal vaginal flora. Due to the inherent limitations of our observational study, we encountered difficulties in fully elucidating the precise mechanism through which BV during the third trimester of pregnancy contributes to a heightened risk of caesarean section and unfavourable maternal outcomes. However, our study revealed a notable disparity in the proportion of caesarean sections attributed to chorioamnionitis between the bacterial vaginosis (BV) group and the nonvaginitis group, with the BV group exhibiting a significantly higher proportion (12.50% vs. 0.00%). Furthermore, the incidence of puerperal infection was 7 times greater in the BV group than in the nonvaginitis group, as indicated by an odds ratio of 7.353 (95% confidence interval: 2.441–22.154, p = 0.000). Therefore, our hypothesis posits that the progression of vaginal pathogens through the reproductive tract may serve as a contributing factor to the adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with bacterial vaginosis. Physiological defence mechanisms, such as cervical mucus plugs and foetal membranes, may have reduced strength before and after induction and delivery. This weakening could facilitate the ascent of vaginal pathogens, leading to the occurrence of intraamniotic or placental inflammation [ – ]. There have been studies showing the presence of intra-amniotic microbiota even in normal pregnancies [ ], but new studies using strict controls do not support this finding [ , ]. Likewise, the prevailing consensus posits that the placenta is a sterile milieu, substantiated by a succession of experiments conducted on atypical pregnancies [ – ]. However, alternative investigations have revealed the presence of diverse bacterial strains within the placental environment [ , ]. Nevertheless, it is anticipated that the amniotic cavity and placenta of a typical pregnancy will exhibit an exceedingly limited microbial biomass, irrespective of bacterial presence. The rupture of membranes may lead to the ascension of vaginal microbes, potentially leading to a swift proliferation of bacteria within the amniotic cavity and placenta. The responses of both the maternal and foetal systems to intrauterine infection encompass the activation of the foetal membrane immune response, the synthesis of prostaglandins, and the release of metalloproteinases [ ]. The presence of BV has been found to be correlated with elevated maternal hs-CRP levels during the initial week following childbirth [ ]. However, the animal studies conducted by Chong Fan1 et al. [ ] revealed the absence of bacteria in the placentas of mice afflicted with severe vaginal infection, thereby implying that adverse pregnancy outcomes may not be attributable to ascending infection as a direct cause. Further investigation is necessary to determine the precise mechanism by which BV in the third trimester contributes to elevated rates of caesarean section following induced labour and negative outcomes for both mothers and infants. Additionally, our study revealed no discernible disparity in caesarean section rates after induction among women with BV and VVC in comparison to those with BV alone. However, it is important to note that these individuals experienced more adverse maternal and foetal outcomes. One potential explanation is that findings from in vitro and in vivo studies suggest that in the context of mixed infections, the colonization and virulence of microorganisms, as well as the immune responses of hosts, are heightened in comparison to those observed in single infections. Additionally, it is posited that clinical phenotypes and adverse outcomes resulting from microorganisms may exhibit greater severity in mixed infections as opposed to single infections [ , ] . Nevertheless, it is imperative to acknowledge the limitations inherent in our study. Initially, to manage expenses, the diagnosis of BV was conducted based on the Amsel criteria. The Amsel criteria method is straightforward and does not necessitate stringent laboratory conditions; however, its sensitivity and specificity are inferior to those of Gram stain microscopy. Furthermore, it was observed that all patients with vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) included in the study exhibited an association with bacterial vaginosis (BV), unlike other studies where the diagnosis of pure VVC was made [ ]. Furthermore, the omission of AV screening in our study was attributed to various constraints. It is worth noting that previous research has reported an AV prevalence ranging from 4.1 to 8.3% during pregnancy. Additionally, our study revealed a low positive rate of GBS, a condition closely linked to AV [ ]. Furthermore, our study was unable to ascertain the impact of bacterial vaginosis (BV) treatment on the outcomes of induced labour. Although prevailing guidelines do not endorse interventions for asymptomatic BV in pregnant women [ ], research conducted by the WHO Global Maternal Sepsis Study

VVC was made [ ]. Furthermore, the omission of AV screening in our study was attributed to various constraints. It is worth noting that previous research has reported an AV prevalence ranging from 4.1 to 8.3% during pregnancy. Additionally, our study revealed a low positive rate of GBS, a condition closely linked to AV [ ]. Furthermore, our study was unable to ascertain the impact of bacterial vaginosis (BV) treatment on the outcomes of induced labour. Although prevailing guidelines do not endorse interventions for asymptomatic BV in pregnant women [ ], research conducted by the WHO Global Maternal Sepsis Study (Gloss) team indicated that screening and managing BV during the third trimester may diminish the probability of unfavourable perinatal consequences [ ]. Mijovic et al. [ ] further documented that timely identification and treatment of vaginal infections resulted in a notable decrease in perinatal morbidity and mortality. In forthcoming research, we intend to conduct randomized controlled trials to assess the efficacy of vaginal rectal screening for bacterial vaginosis in gestational weeks 35 to 37, along with subsequent treatment [ ]. The primary objective of this study was to ascertain whether the implementation of screening and subsequent treatment for bacterial vaginosis during the third trimester of pregnancy can effectively mitigate the risk of unfavourable perinatal outcomes. Conclusions The elevated prevalence of BV among women who underwent induced labour during the third trimester of pregnancy was found to be correlated with an increased rate of caesarean section and unfavourable outcomes for both the mother and foetus. Furthermore, the presence of mixed infection involving both BV and VVC further exacerbated the negative maternal and foetal outcomes. Hence, it is imperative to allocate additional attention to patients with BV during the third trimester of pregnancy. Further investigation is warranted to explore the efficacy of BV screening and clinical intervention during the late stages of pregnancy. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1. documents.title: Newborn Care Up to Six Days Birth

chunks.content: Background Consequences of excess gestational weight gain (GWG) The documented adverse sequelae of excess GWG for both mother and child include undesirable pregnancy/birth outcomes and/or later health outcomes that are likely to impose a substantive downstream burden on healthcare costs [ ]. The most common adverse effect of excessive GWG on maternal health is weight retention (five months and even up to three years postpartum) [ – ]. Mothers entering subsequent pregnancies at a higher weight are at greater risk for long-term obesity and future co-morbidities such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease [ , ]. The emerging evidence of developmental origins of health and disease implicates the impact of mothers’ health during pregnancy on “programming” of the growing fetus in utero to develop adverse health outcomes [ , ]. Maternal excess GWG has been reported as the strongest predictor of obesity in the offspring [ – ]. The use of low-fat dairy foods as the source of protein in pregnancy is proposed based on studies in animals [ ] and humans [ – ] that provide support for the putative effects of components of dairy foods such as calcium and leucine as anti-adipogenic and pro-lipolytic agents. Consumption of high dairy protein may not only benefit GWG but also improve other maternal pregnancy outcomes such as dysglycemia, elevated blood pressure, blood lipid profiles, and risk of pre-eclampsia, the latter due to higher intake of calcium and vitamin D [ ]. Guidelines for GWG exist and have been interpreted for practice in Canada [ , ]. Until there is evidence of effective population level interventions to assist women in achieving healthy weights, programs aimed at interventions during pregnancy to improve weight management and pregnancy outcomes are a starting point. Pregnancy has been described as a “teachable moment” for weight control and obesity prevention in women [ ]. The most convincing approach to achieve reduction in GWG is the combination of physical activity and diet counseling, preferably in combination with weight monitoring [ , , ]. Yet current clinical practice guidelines for managing GWG are not founded on randomized trials and lack specific “active intervention ingredients” [ ] that are proven effective in achieving target GWG. Maternal programming of bone health Findings from epidemiological and animal studies support a role for the programming of fetal, neonatal, and adult bone outcomes in response to exposures during pregnancy such as maternal nutrition and other lifestyle variables [ – ]. In three longitudinal observational studies, maternal intake of dairy foods during pregnancy was associated with higher bone mass in offspring aged 6–16 years [ – ]. In prospective cohort studies, maternal physical activity level has also been positively associated with infant bone mass and geometry at birth [ , ]. Being born with optimal bone mass may have long-term benefits since childhood bone mass tracks until skeletal maturity, when peak bone mass is achieved [ ]. Collectively, these findings suggest that bone mass during childhood and adolescence may be predictive of an individual’s risk for osteoporosis, as peak bone mass is a strong predictor of osteoporotic fracture later in life [ ]. To date, only one randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a small sample ( N = 36) investigated the effect of dairy product supplementation on bone mineral density (BMD) and bone turn-over in pregnant women and these women entered pregnancy with a habitually low calcium intake [ ]. The study showed a beneficial effect of increased milk consumption on maternal bone mass density at the spine and on suppression of bone resorption when measured at 6 ± 1 weeks postpartum. While promising, further studies are needed with larger sample sizes and evaluation of bone health outcomes in the offspring. In addition, no study to date has investigated the impact of dairy product supplementation during pregnancy on bone health outcomes of women after delivery. Informed by our recent clinical and qualitative research, as well as existing systematic reviews, we have designed a RCT comprising several unique features with the objective of controlling GWG and optimizing bone health of mother and infant. We will test the effectiveness of a novel structured and monitored nutrition (high-protein dairy-based diet) along with an exercise (walking) intervention that is science-based, vetted for feasibility in pregnant women and care providers through focus groups, in pregnant women of most pre-pregnancy weight categories (except extreme obesity) in a community setting (as opposed to hospital-based). Specific objectives and hypothesis The primary research objective of the Be Healthy in Pregnancy (BHIP) study is to determine whether introducing a structured and monitored nutrition (high-dairy protein diet) and exercise (walking) program (intervention) in early pregnancy, compared to standard prenatal care (control), will increase the number of women attaining GWG (outcome) within the Institute of Medicine (IOM) recommendations for their pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) sub-category [ ]. Secondary

for feasibility in pregnant women and care providers through focus groups, in pregnant women of most pre-pregnancy weight categories (except extreme obesity) in a community setting (as opposed to hospital-based). Specific objectives and hypothesis The primary research objective of the Be Healthy in Pregnancy (BHIP) study is to determine whether introducing a structured and monitored nutrition (high-dairy protein diet) and exercise (walking) program (intervention) in early pregnancy, compared to standard prenatal care (control), will increase the number of women attaining GWG (outcome) within the Institute of Medicine (IOM) recommendations for their pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) sub-category [ ]. Secondary objectives include determination of the impact of a maternal high-dairy diet with exercise compared to standard care diet during pregnancy on: (1) bone status (e.g. blood biomarkers procollagen type I that contains N-terminal extensions (PINP), C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) in mothers during pregnancy; (2) infant bone status at birth via cord blood; and (3) mother and infant bone status at six months postpartum by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan. The over-arching hypothesis is that maternal consumption of a high-dairy diet during pregnancy will have a positive impact on: (1) GWG; (2) bone health status of the mother during and after pregnancy; and (3) bone mass and bone size of the offspring, after adjustment for factors known to influence skeletal status. Methods/design Trial design The BHIP study is a two-arm, two-site prospective RCT. This study is designed as a prospective superiority trial, with 1:1 allocation ratio to either the Intervention group (i.e. Nutrition + Exercise intervention: high-dairy nutrition intervention combined with structured exercise) or the Control group (i.e. usual care as per National Health Canada recommendations) during pregnancy. The study is open-label with blinded endpoints. The study protocol is described following the standard protocol items: recommendations for interventional trials (SPIRIT) guidelines [ ]. See Additional file for the SPIRIT checklist and Additional file for the WHO trial registration data set. The core BHIP trial follows women up to delivery as the primary outcome relates to GWG. The Bone-BHIP study is an extension of the core BHIP trial that continues a follow-up of the women and their offspring until six months after delivery, with the objective to assess maternal and infant bone status. This trial is registered at ClinicalTrial.gov ( NCT01689961 ). The BHIP trial is conducted by collaborative research teams at McMaster University (Hamilton, ON) and Western University (London, ON) in Canada. The study takes place in academic hospitals and community healthcare clinics in London, Burlington, and Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. Recruitment is facilitated by healthcare professionals (e.g. family doctors and midwives) who ask their patients for consent to be contacted by the BHIP study team, as well as poster advertisements in midwifery, family practice, and ultrasound clinics, at community sites such as the YMCA, libraries, and coffee shops, and on Facebook or Kijiji. Study recruitment began in January 2013 and is expected to be completed by April 2018, reaching the a priori calculated sample size of 242 participants for our primary outcome. All participants who sign consent to contact forms receive a phone call by study personnel and are provided a general overview of the study and expectations using a scripted text. Figure outlines the participant’s timeline in the BHIP study. Participants are screened for eligibility during the telephone interview according to the criteria list below. Eligible women are enrolled in the study and sign informed consent by the end of the first trimester of pregnancy (i.e. 12–17 weeks of gestation). The flow diagram (Fig. ) will be included in future published results. This study is open-label due to the nature of the intervention. The study research assistants (data collectors) administering the personalized Nutrition + Exercise intervention are not blinded to group allocation. In addition, the participants are not blinded to their own group allocation, in order to maximize adherence to the lifestyle treatment. Mothers randomized to the intervention and control groups are assessed at the study clinic on different days, to prevent interaction between participants of each study arm. The primary data outcome collector is blinded to group allocation and is conducting the study visits for all participants, regardless of their group allocation. To maximize the objectivity of findings, the primary outcome assessor and data analysts/statistician are blinded to the study allocation and are not collecting any study data. Interventions All participants receive usual care as delivered by their healthcare practitioner (family physician or midwife) during pregnancy. In addition, after enrolment in the RCT and regardless of their group allocation, all participants receive counseling by the study nutritionist on the latest recommendations by Health Canada as published online ( https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/healthy-living/healthy-pregnancy.html ). After delivery, both study groups receive usual care from their healthcare practitioners with no further intervention; the research team prospectively follows participants at three months and six months postpartum. Table outlines the study arms. Participants randomized to the personalized, monitored, and structured Nutrition + Exercise program group (intervention) begin early in the second trimester of their pregnancy until the end of pregnancy with counseling on a weekly or biweekly basis (Table and Fig. ). The nutrition component is an individualized nutrition plan tailored to each participant’s energy requirements with a high protein content (25% protein energy) provided primarily by dairy foods. Dairy foods are accepted by women during pregnancy as a healthy choice as indicated from our pilot study [ ] and in a recent birth cohort study in the same community in which women consumed an average of ≥ 3 servings of dairy foods per day [ ]. Dairy foods are sources of high-quality proteins, calcium, and vitamin D in the case of milk as it is under mandatory fortification with vitamin D in Canada. The Nutrition + Exercise intervention is considered safe. First, the nutrient intake associated with the increased low-fat dairy consumption is less than the tolerable upper intake level for all nutrients as recommended per the Dietary Reference Intake by Health Canada. In addition, walking (the exercise component) is the easiest physical activity to undertake and implement in terms of goal-setting for step count and monitoring adherence using accelerometer-type devices as demonstrated in our previous studies [ – ]. Walking was the most practical exercise intervention of choice since women reduce moderate and vigorous physical activity during pregnancy yet maintain levels of walking [ ]. Most importantly, these exercise guidelines are based on the Physical Activity Readiness Medical Examination (PARmed-X) for Pregnancy [ ]. Data from the Nutrition and Exercise Lifestyle Intervention Program study [ ] indicates that the goal of 10,000 daily steps is feasible under free-living conditions and has been effectively utilized in a number of trials [ ]. A component of the intervention is discontinued if the medical condition of a participant changes and the intervention is modified if a participant requests a change due to personal reasons, such as food aversion or pain episode. The intervention is personalized for every woman, to ensure the goal of 25% energy from protein and 10,000 steps/day are achieved. Additionally, estimated energy requirements are calculated for each mother using the equation derived in the Dietary Reference Intake report for normal and overweight women [ ] with energy intakes adjusted as recommended in the second and third trimesters [ ]. The individualized nutrition plan is fashioned upon a standard three-day food intake record completed by the mothers that includes one weekend day as used previously in pregnant women [ ]. The individualized nutrition plans and counseling are conducted by a study nutritionist providing the number of food servings to meet their estimated energy requirements. The nutrition plan is modified if GWG monitoring indicates weight loss or excess gain has occurred as recommended in the GWG guidelines [ , ]. Adverse events related to the intervention are reported to our local ethics boards. Other non-intervention-related adverse events are noted in the participant’s chart and monitored, in accordance with the N2 Network of Networks guidelines Canada [ ]. Several strategies are used to improve adherence to the intervention. For the exercise component, participants wear and track their step counts on a weekly basis, increasing motivation and adherence to the treatment. In addition, they go for a walk with the research staff and have a personalized counseling session with the study nutritionist. For the nutrition component, participants are provided with low-fat milk, cottage cheese, and/or yogurt, as per their preference, to ensure they consume the recommended amount of dairy foods. Participants come to the study site at least every other week to receive their dairy foods and the study nutritionist shares strategies and recipes with the participants to ensure they consume the targeted amount of dairy food servings. All these actions improved the adherence to the study protocol. Participants randomized to the usual care group (control) receive usual prenatal care. Participants are given the most recent advice from Health Canada including Healthy Weight Gain During Pregnancy [ ], the Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator [ ], and Eating Well with Canada’s Food Guide [ ]. Mothers are followed by their primary care provider who also receives the same Health Canada materials. After delivery, they are followed by their healthcare practitioners. In addition, the control participants are invited to participate in a focus group and to attend an information session led by a midwife; topics discussed include pain relief options during labor and breastfeeding techniques (Table ). Fasted maternal blood samples for metabolic and bone health biomarkers are collected at 12–17 weeks of gestation, 36–38 weeks of gestation, and at six months postpartum; venous cord blood is collected at delivery. Serum is collected in serum-separating with gel (SST™) vacutainers and in spray-coated silica vacutainers; plasma is collected in sodium fluoride/ Na 2 ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (Na2EDTA) vacutainers. Sample are centrifuged for 10 min at 3000 rpm at 4 °C; serum separator tubes are spun for an additional 5 min, aliquoted, and stored at − 80 °C. Samples are batched to include all samples from each mother for analysis in our laboratories when participants have completed the study. Fasting plasma glucose is determined using a hexokinase photometric assay (Architect kit, Abbott, Abbott Park, IL, USA). Serum triglycerides are analyzed using a glycerol phosphate oxidase photometric assay (Architect kit, Abbott, Abbott Park, IL, USA) completed by Hamilton Health Sciences Regional Laboratory Medicine Program. Serum leptin and insulin are analyzed using Luminex® human premixed multi-analyte enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit supplied by R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN, USA). Serum adiponectin and C-reactive protein are analyzed by Luminex® premixed multi-analyte ELISA kit supplied by R&D Systems. Bone formation is assessed by measuring serum PINP by ELISA (Cloud Clone Corp., Houston, TX, USA). Bone resorption is assessed by measuring serum CTX-I by (Serum Crosslaps (CTX-1) ELISA, product code AC-02F1 Immunodiagnostic Systems, UK). Growth is assessed by measuring serum IGF-1 by ELISA (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA). All standards and samples are analyzed in duplicate, following the manufacturer’s instructions. A serum quality control is run in triplicate at the beginning and end of each ELISA plate to calculate inter- and intra-assay coefficients of variability. Serum vitamin D metabolites are measured by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) using a Waters AQUITY Tandem Quadropole Detector coupled to an AQUITY UPLC system (Waters Corporation), after extraction that includes a saponification step as adapted from Hymoller [ ]. Accuracy is determined using the certified Vitamin D analytes serum-based standard reference material (SRM 972a) from the US National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST; National Bureau of Standards, Washington, DC, USA) [ ]. Precision is measured using a serum quality control in all runs of samples tested, allowing calculation of inter- and intra-assay coefficients of variability. DNA extracted from maternal and cord blood plasma samples will be purified using the Chemagen 500 MSM I (PerkinElmer chemagen Technologie GmbH, Baesweiler, Germany) and genotyped using the Human Core Exome Bead Chip by Illumina. The chip is specifically designed to allow imputation of up to 18 million markers in multi-ethnic populations. Data cleaning and quality control of SNPs data are done according to the guidelines published by Winkler et al. [ ]. It also allows for verification of the instrument stability over the course of the study. Statistical methods The analysis and reporting of the results will follow the SPIRIT statement for reporting RCTs [ ]. The process of patient selection and flow throughout the study will be summarized using a flow-diagram (Fig. ). The results of patient baseline characteristics and outcome variables (both primary and secondary) will be summarized using descriptive summary measures: expressed as mean (standard deviation) or median (range) for continuous variables and n (%) for categorical variables. All statistical tests will be performed using two-sided tests at the 0.05 level of significance. Binary outcomes will be analyzed using logistic regression and continuous outcomes will be analyzed using linear regression. All analyses will account for stratification by including study site and participants’ BMI category in the models. For all models, the results will be expressed as estimate of the difference for continuous outcomes (odds ratio [OR] or relative risk [RR] for binary outcomes), corresponding two-sided 95% confidence intervals (CI) and associated p values. P values will be reported to three decimal places with values < 0.001 reported as < 0.001. The Hosmer–Lemshow will be used to assess goodness-of-fit for logistic regression and explore the residuals to assess goodness-of-fit and model assumptions for linear regression. An intention-to-treat principle will be adopted to analyze all outcomes. Multiple-imputation will also be used to handle missing data during data collection. Sensitivity analyses will be performed using some of the commonly used RCT patient-level methods (e.g. generalized estimating equations, the random-effect model which account for the potential correlation within sites, etc.) to assess the robustness of the results [ ]. All the analyses will be done using SAS 9.2 (Cary, NC, USA) or SPSS 13 (Chicago, IL, USA). Table provides a summary of the planned methods of analyses for each outcome and subgroup. Power calculation The sample size calculation for the core study is based on the test of the null hypothesis that the percentages of women with GWG within IOM guidelines in the two populations (intervention and control) are equal. To account for the uncertainty in these prior estimates, we calculated the sample size for different values of the percentage of women with weight within IOM guidelines in the control group in the range of 50–65%, with a risk difference of 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30%. While initially we targeted a total sample size of 350, the constraints of our funding timelines (which include a one-year CHIR grant extension) and a recruitment rate that was less than projected despite our best efforts, we revised our desired sample size to 242. Based on our a priori calculation, a sample size 111 per group corresponds to an absolute difference of 30% with our Nutrition + Exercise intervention, resulting in 30% of women in the treatment group having a GWG exceeding the IOM recommendations compared to 65% in the control group. Discussion The BHIP study is novel as it proposes a feasible Nutrition + Exercise intervention that pregnant women could incorporate into their lifestyle and improve adherence to GWG recommendations. In addition, it will contribute to the knowledge of the perinatal developmental programming of body composition and skeletal phenotypes. The BHIP RCT enrolls women in early pregnancy (12–17 weeks of gestation). Ideally, women should have access to general health interventions before pregnancy; however, currently pregnancy is often the first opportunity for health professionals to address issues beyond those directly related to the pregnancy state. Thus, one of the strengths of the BHIP study is that it starts in early pregnancy and monitors participants until six months postpartum. In addition, measures of health outcomes in both mother and child at various time points throughout pregnancy and postpartum allow for a comprehensive evaluation of the intervention effects. Lastly, one particular strength of the BHIP study is the individualized intervention and weekly monitoring. Evidence shows that the consumption of dairy foods (nutrition component) is well accepted during pregnancy [ ], while walking (exercise component) is the best physical activity to promote adherence during pregnancy [ – ]. The primary outcome of GWG was selected because it is the key clinical problem we are addressing with our Nutrition + Exercise intervention. Pre-pregnancy obesity and excess GWG are the strongest maternal characteristics associated with offspring obesity [ , , ] and childhood metabolic dysfunction [ ]. Excess GWG in pregnancy is a major clinical challenge affecting Canadian women who enter pregnancy overweight and even women of normal pre-pregnancy weight [ , ]. At the national level, a cross-sectional study on pregnancy experiences in Canada determined that over one-third of women entered pregnancy overweight or obese and nearly 60% experienced GWG greater than that recommended by the IOM recommendations for GWG [ ]. The Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition prospective cohort study reported similar statistics with a greater number of overweight and obese women (80%) gaining excess weight during pregnancy [ ]. Likewise, in the Hamilton region, data from the Family Atherosclerosis Monitoring In earLY life birth cohort demonstrated that > 50% of women entered pregnancy with a pre-pregnancy BMI of > 25.0 kg/m 2 and > 50% exceeded the IOM guidelines for GWG [ ]. Evidence to date suggest that the most convincing approach to achieve appropriate GWG is an intervention combining physical activity and nutrition, in combination with weight monitoring [ , , ]. The secondary outcome of bone status was selected due to the emerging evidence of risk of osteoporosis in later life being programmed from the womb [ ]. Bone biomarkers were selected as outcomes following the International Osteoporosis Foundation and the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine recommendations, which is to measure a marker of bone formation and a marker of bone resorption to assess bone turnover [ ]. Currently, the most sensitive markers recommended are subgroups of type I collagen representing the predominant component of the bone matrix wherein sub-products can be measured as markers of formation and resorption of the bone [ ]. as outcomes following the International Osteoporosis Foundation and the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine recommendations, which is to measure a marker of bone formation and a marker of bone resorption to assess bone turnover [ ]. Currently, the most sensitive markers recommended are subgroups of type I collagen representing the predominant component of the bone matrix wherein sub-products can be measured as markers of formation and resorption of the bone [ ]. To support fetal bone growth, pregnant women undergo bone metabolic adaptations over the course of pregnancy, where bone resorption usually rises and formation declines [ ]. These changes result in high bone turnover during pregnancy [ ]. Maternal bone turnover peaks during the third trimester, with a marked increase in bone resorption observed at 38 weeks of gestation [ ]. Based on this knowledge, two biomarkers of bone modelling are quantified in maternal blood at 36–38 weeks of gestation and in cord blood. The marker of bone formation is PINP and the marker of bone resorption is CTX-I. Blood samples are consistently collected in a fasted state and in the morning, as suggested by the National Bone Health Alliance [ ]. In addition, vitamin D status is measured by serum 25(OH)D as it plays an important role in calcium homeostasis and bone metabolism [ ] and is a reflection of dietary vitamin D intake and sun exposure. Both the frequency of milk consumption and sun exposure were shown to be positive predictors of serum 25(OH)D concentrations in the recent multivariate analysis of three cycles of the Canadian Community Health Measures surveys [ ]. The active form of vitamin D, 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D, is also measured since it is known to be upregulated during pregnancy [ ]. Bone mineral content was selected as an outcome because it is linked to the peak bone mass (i.e. highest bone mass accrued for an individual) and is predictive of osteoporotic fracture [ ]. Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that childhood BMC persists until peak bone mass and could indicate individuals at risk of osteoporotic fracture [ ]. The nature of the intervention brings a limitation; the research study personnel in direct contact with the participants are not blinded to the study allocation of each participant. To preserve the integrity of the study findings and the internal validity of the study, all other investigators and statisticians are blinded to the study allocation, including people collecting and performing the analysis of primary and secondary outcomes. Some sources of bias are inevitable in the context of the study: recruitment sites are mostly primary care clinics, with few participants recruited from advertisements in the community. Since women are excluded with limited comprehension of the English language, if documented signs of depression or a pre-pregnancy BMI > 40 kg/m 2 , the generalization of the study would exclude such groups. From previous studies completed in urban Southern Ontario [ , ] we anticipate that our study population will be mostly Caucasian, holding a university degree, and with a medium to high socioeconomic status. This sample is representative of the populations in the cities were recruitment occurred as they are modern urban centers with universities, colleges, and major commerce. Thus, the results will be generalizable to populations of women living in many Canadian cities with academic centers and major commerce. In addition, our results will still be of high value for the general Canadian pregnant women population who are served through provincial public health units, as it will bring new knowledge to refine the Canada Prenatal Nutrition Program (CPNP, https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/health-promotion/childhood-adolescence/programs-initiatives/canada-prenatal-nutrition-program-cpnp.html ), which is currently offered through public health but not based on evidence. The strengths of the design include that the Nutrition + Exercise intervention was vetted for feasibility in pregnant women and care providers through focus groups and was conducted in pregnant women of all pre-pregnancy BMI categories (except extreme obesity) and in a community setting (as opposed to hospital-based as in many reported studies). For the timely recruitment of study participants, challenges included prolonged ethics approval processes at secondary recruitment sites, reduced recruitment at community family practices due to influx of immigrants who were non-English speaking (thus not eligible), and competition with other studies sampling pregnant women. In light of these, we have taken measures to achieve the predetermined sample size based on a power analysis for the primary outcome so that the integrity of the study is preserved and the results are able to properly test the stated hypothesis and provide the needed new knowledge. To expand recruitment at McMaster University a new local study site was set up in a nearby city, Burlington, Ontario, with the collaboration of midwifery and obstetric clinics, as well as the local hospital. To maximize retention of participants, we implemented a number of procedures such as study visit times at the convenience of the participants, including home visits. We also offered in-person, over the phone, and email correspondence to keep participants engaged. For participants in the intervention group, providing them with the dairy products (which are an integral part of the intervention) increases the likelihood of consuming the recommended amount. For the exercise component, participants receive a free pedometer as a self-motivation tool to reach their step count goals. Lastly, for both groups, participants are compensated on three occasions with $25 gift cards that they can redeem at a local grocery store. If effective, this RCT will generate high-quality evidence to refine the nutrition guidelines during pregnancy to improve health of women during pregnancy and their offspring in early life, including acquisition of a strong skeleton. Trial status Active recruitment continues since a no-cost extension of one year from CIHR was obtained in December 2016, to allow the BHP study to achieve the target sample size.
